title: ÆTHER: Refreshing Sway (from First Love v7, natural)
story: A fresh, breezy morning: the same six-part journey and steady 6/8 sway Jithesh liked in First Love v7, now as a refreshing track, not a romance.

brief.notes: Jithesh 29 Oct 18:54-18:58: First Love v7 takes 1 and 2 are not romantic but the six-part pattern is really good; keep both as refreshing tracks for a future edit, not locked. Fixes: tumbi, flute etc. used unnaturally; heavy echo destroys the natural sound and originality; DJ-style work and pauses break the natural rhythm. 'Keep it natural, keep it rhythmic.' This keeps v7's six-part map and single steady 6/8 sway (pulse 0.55-0.68 measured on take 2) with a dry live-room sound per music-scoring.md rule 16: no echo, no glitch-chopped veena, no reversed swells, no drop-outs. Prompt mode (music_v2).

prompt: SOUND MUST BE NATURAL: a dry, close, natural acoustic recording of real musicians playing together in one room, like a live South Indian film-studio session: no echo, no delay, no big reverb, no effects, no filter sweeps, no glitch or chopped sounds, no reversed sounds, no stutters, no electronic DJ tricks, no pauses, breaks or drop-outs between sections; every instrument sounds exactly like itself, played by hand. A bright, refreshing, breezy instrumental in the style of South Indian film music, like a fresh morning breeze through coconut palms, a walk by the river at sunrise: light, happy, playful, uplifting, carefree. Not romantic, not sad, not a festival, not heroic. Raga Kalyani (Yaman), a major scale with a raised fourth, sung-style phrasing with gamakam slides and quick natural ornaments. Instruments, all acoustic and natural: a bamboo flute plays the main melody with a real breath sound; a solo violin answers; a bright tumbi plucks short natural playful riffs, never processed; a santoor plays clean cascades; a mandolin and a fingerpicked acoustic guitar keep a light strum; a plucked veena played naturally; soft strings underneath; glass bangles and a little ghungroo for sparkle; tabla and dholak for the rhythm, with a round acoustic bass. RHYTHM IS THE PRIORITY: from 6 s to the last 3 seconds a clear, steady, flowing 6/8 sway like a boat rocking, about 66 dotted-quarter beats per minute, tabla and dholak in the front, never stopping, never thinning out, never pausing; the same tempo all through, the groove only grows a little fuller part by part. Six parts: 0-6 s: the flute alone plays a rising three-note call (root, major third, fifth) over a soft tanpura, then the tabla starts. 6-18 s: light tabla sway, flute and violin trade short cheerful question-and-answer phrases, the tumbi winks in. 18-32 s: the full sway; the flute sings the main bright melody, the mandolin and guitar strum along, santoor answers. 32-46 s: the tabla swings busier; the violin takes the melody, then flute and violin play it together in harmony. 46-58 s: an interlude: santoor cascades and a quick flute and violin duet with natural Carnatic flourishes, the sway still driving underneath. 58-76 s: the fullest part: dholak joins with joyful fills on the same sway, the tumbi bounces, everyone plays the main melody together, bright and fresh. 76-80 s: the flute plays the opening three-note call once more and resolves home over the last tabla phrase. Absolutely no echo, no delay, no reverb tails, no glitch, no reversed swells, no risers, no DJ-style breaks, no EDM, no side-chain pumping, no silence anywhere.
